description: In 1818, an 18-year-old Mary Shelley wrote the first great science-fiction novel. Victor Frankenstein creates life, then runs from his creature: a fable about science without ethics.

hero.hook: A night of storms, a bet between poets, and the myth of the modern Prometheus.

blocks.text: Published in **1818**, **Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus** is usually called the first great work of **science fiction**. **Mary Shelley** was only **18** when she wrote it, at the meeting point of dark **[[Romanticism]]** and the scientific arguments of her time.

Victor Frankenstein and his nameless being are more than gothic horror figures. They raise a lasting question: what becomes of a mind that is manufactured and then abandoned? The novel weighs **[[The creator's responsibility]]**: you cannot make a life without answering for what follows.

In **1816**, the eruption of **Mount Tambora** in Indonesia plunged Europe into the **[[Year Without a Summer (1816)]]**: gray skies, ruined harvests, an end-of-the-world mood. Mary Shelley was staying at the **Villa Diodati**, on the shore of Lake Geneva, with **Percy Shelley** and **Lord Byron**. To fight off the boredom, Byron proposed a contest of frightening stories.

blocks.caption: Mary Shelley, author of a myth that reaches far beyond gothic horror
The Villa Diodati: Frankenstein born in the storms of 1816

blocks.text: John Polidori, Byron's doctor, also wrote at Diodati the story that founded the modern vampire, long before Dracula.

Mary Shelley drew on **[[galvanism]]**, the experiments that seemed to wake the muscles of corpses. In a waking dream she saw a student standing before a creature that came to life in front of him. Alone among the guests, she carried the bet through to the end and produced a masterpiece.

sections.title: The laboratory by Lake Geneva: an apocalyptic birth

blocks.text: **Victor Frankenstein** embodies **[[Hubris]]**: the ambition that defies the natural order. At **Ingolstadt** he hunts for the “secret of life,” not to get rich, but to become a **modern Prometheus**, like the Greek titan who stole fire from the gods. The moment his creature wakes, the dream turns into a nightmare.

blocks.caption: Shelley's creature: terrifying, but above all eloquent and aware

blocks.text: Victor flees in disgust at the ugliness of what he has made. He abandons his artificial “son,” and it is that cowardice, rather than the act of creation itself, that sets the tragedy going. Shelley shows that science without conscience condemns the creator as surely as the creature it rejects.

What makes the novel original is the voice of the creature. Intelligent and eloquent, it learns by watching a peasant family and by reading **[[Paradise Lost]]** by **Milton**. Born “good,” a **[[tabula rasa]]** in the philosophical sense, it is corrupted by the violent rejection of every human it meets.
I am malicious because I am miserable.

It asks for a companion so that it will not suffer alone. Victor refuses out of fear. So the creature destroys everything he loves, until his loneliness matches its own. The novel becomes a meditation on **[[social determinism]]**: a society sometimes manufactures its monsters by shutting out whoever is different.

sections.title: The creature wakes: a mind with no name

blocks.text: The novel ends in the **Arctic**, Victor dead, the creature vanishing into the fog with a promise to destroy itself. Today “Frankenstein” names any technology that escapes its inventor: genetically modified organisms, artificial intelligence, gene editing. Shelley saw **[[posthumanism]]** coming.
In popular culture the monster is often called “Frankenstein.” In fact Frankenstein is the creator: the being has no name at all, a sign that Victor refused to be its father.
**Frankenstein** is a reminder that you cannot create a life without answering for what follows. The real monster is not ugliness. It is the abandonment of what you brought into the world.

sections.title: A modern myth and its universal afterlife
